# Nested Quantifiers

## More Than One

Friday we bound one variable. Nothing stops us binding two.

\

|      $\forall x\, \forall y\ \text{Knows}(x,y)$

\

|      $\forall x\, \exists y\ \text{Knows}(x,y)$

\

|      $\exists x\, \forall y\ \text{Knows}(x,y)$

\

Say each one out loud. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
Everybody knows everybody. / Everybody knows somebody. / Somebody knows
everybody.

The third is the one worth slowing on -- it is a claim about ONE person, and it
is much stronger than the second. That is the whole lecture in one slide, so do
not resolve it yet; just let them hear that two and three are different.
:::

## Every Lock Has a Key {.smaller}

$K(k, l)$: key $k$ opens lock $l$.

::: {.fillable}
| | Says what, in English? |
|---|---|
| $\forall l\, \exists k\ K(k,l)$ | |
| $\exists k\, \forall l\ K(k,l)$ | |
:::

\

Which one would a locksmith charge you more for? \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
Top: every lock has some key that opens it. Ordinary.
Bottom: there is one key that opens every lock. A MASTER KEY.

Same two symbols, same relation, swapped order -- and one of them is worth
paying for. Nobody needs convincing that these differ once it is a master key.

Then the direction that does hold: a master key IS a key for each lock, so the
bottom gives you the top. The top gives you nothing about the bottom.
:::

## Does Order Matter? {.smaller}

::: {.fillable}
| Swap | Same? |
|---|:-:|
| $\forall x\, \forall y\ P(x,y)$ &emsp; vs &emsp; $\forall y\, \forall x\ P(x,y)$ | |
| $\exists x\, \exists y\ P(x,y)$ &emsp; vs &emsp; $\exists y\, \exists x\ P(x,y)$ | |
| $\forall x\, \exists y\ P(x,y)$ &emsp; vs &emsp; $\exists y\, \forall x\ P(x,y)$ | |
:::

\

So the rule is: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
Yes, yes, NO.

Two quantifiers of the SAME kind commute freely. Two of DIFFERENT kinds do not.
Verified exhaustively over every relation on a three-element domain.

And the asymmetry is one-way:

    exists y forall x  ==>  forall x exists y        always
    forall x exists y  ==>  exists y forall x        NOT

Of the 512 relations on a domain of three, 174 satisfy the second and fail the
first. It is the common case, not a curiosity.
:::

## One Picture {.smaller}

Rows are $x$, columns are $y$. A mark means $P(x,y)$ holds.

::: {.fillable}
| | $y_1$ | $y_2$ | $y_3$ |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| $x_1$ | | | ✓ |
| $x_2$ | | | ✓ |
| $x_3$ | | ✓ | |
:::

\

Every row has a mark, so \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

No column is all marks, so \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
forall x exists y  is TRUE -- every row has something.
exists y forall x  is FALSE -- no single column is full.

This is the picture to keep. "Everyone has one" is a statement about ROWS.
"One works for everyone" is a statement about COLUMNS. Swapping the quantifiers
swaps which way you read the grid, and a grid can easily have every row covered
with no column full.

Draw the master key on it: a master key is a FULL COLUMN.
:::

## Your Turn {.activity}

In pairs, work the worksheet.

\

Page 3 is the grid you just saw — except now **you** place the hearts.

{{< countdown minutes=25 >}}

::: notes
activities/lecture-09_activity.pdf, four pages, linked from the schedule.

  1  Eight students, seven predicates. For five statements: English, truth
     value, and the NEGATION. The negations are the part that will slow them.
  2  They write their own -- one true, one false, two predicates minimum,
     plus negations.
  3  Hero/Villain grids. Place hearts to realise a statement using AS FEW AS
     POSSIBLE, then judge statements against a given grid.
  4  A new quantifier meaning "there exists exactly 2". Minimum and maximum
     hearts to make each statement true.

Page 3 is One Picture made constructive: reading a grid is easy, BUILDING the
sparsest one that satisfies forall-exists forces them to notice it needs one
mark per row, while exists-forall forces a whole column. Point back to the
slide when you set them off.

Page 4 is the good one, and it is the reason not to rush. "Exactly 2" is a
quantifier they have never met, and min/max makes them reason about the SHAPE
of a satisfying grid rather than recall a rule.

TIMING. Four pages is more than the slot holds. Roughly 25 minutes gets them
through 1 and 3. If you want page 4 -- and it is the most interesting -- cut
page 2, which is the most easily set as homework.
:::
